--- title: "ASM Chapter 5" author: "Dr Alun ap Rhisiart" date: "2026-10-21" categories: [code, julia, statistics, asm, ecology] execute: echo: true warning: false output: true engine: julia --- Chapter 5 of Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists, by Marc Kéry and Kenneth Kellner, focuses on Ordinary Linear Regression. This chapter also gets in the interesting subject of Posterior Predictive Checks and Goodness Of Fit. In this chapter, we use a simulated dataset about wallcreepers (which we don't have in the UK, grrrh). I guess this is very familiar to most people. If the value of our dependent variable $y_i$ varies according to independent variable $x_i$, then $$\mu = \alpha + \beta\cdot x_i$$ We take this to deterministic, linear part to be the mean, or expected value. $$y_i\sim{Normal(\alpha + \beta\cdot x_i, \sigma^2)}$$ We can also express this as a linear equation for the mean plus an error term. $$y_i = \alpha + \beta\cdot x_i + \epsilon_i$$ $$\epsilon_i\sim{Normal(0, \sigma^2)}$$ So, we have an overall intercept, a coefficient for the effect of x, which will be a regression line, and some scatter around that line which is normally distributed but centered on the line itself. ## 5.2 Data generation As usual, the data is simulated, so we know the real value of the parameters, and can check that our model can recover them. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 16 # number of years var = 25 # residual variance truth = (α = 40, β = -0.5, σ = sqrt(var)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (α = 40, β = -0.5, σ = 5.0) ``` ::: ::: Next, we plot the generated data. As in previous chapters, although we can get random numbers from the Normal distribution, they won't exactly match the book output, because it is a different RNG. So we will just drop into R to get the value of epsilon. I fudged putting the sd into R because R doesn't know Unicode; I could just use roman letters (eps) for the variable, but it isn't important here, since I just want to get the same numbers. In reality, I would use the Julia RNG anyway. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using RCall @rput n R"set.seed(5);eps <- rnorm(n, 0, sd = 5)" @rget eps ``` ::: ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using StatsPlots, Distributions ϵ = eps x = 1:n y = @. truth.α + truth.β * x + ϵ scatter(1989 .+ x, y, xlabel="Year", ylabel="Wallcreeper Count", title="Simulated Wallcreeper Data") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 5.3 Analysis with Canned Functions in Julia This section is going to fit a linear regression model to the simulated wallcreeper data using Julia's built-in functions. ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using GLM, StatsBase data = (; x = x, y = y) model = lm(@formula(y ~ x), data) model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` StatsModels.TableRegressionModel{LinearModel{GLM.LmResp{Vector{Float64}}, GLM.DensePredChol{Float64, LinearAlgebra.CholeskyPivoted{Float64, Matrix{Float64}, Vector{Int64}}}}, Matrix{Float64}} y ~ 1 + x Coefficients: ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Coef. Std. Error t Pr(>|t|) Lower 95% Upper 95% ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (Intercept) 40.7426 2.40168 16.96 <1e-10 35.5915 45.8937 x -0.690722 0.248376 -2.78 0.0147 -1.22344 -0.158009 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ``` ::: ::: ### 5.3.2 Goodness-of-fit assessment THe book prints out the residuals, which we can do also, but it also gives the code, but not the plot, of a histogram. I'll display it here, although it isn't that useful for such a small dataset. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} histogram(residuals(model), bins = 20, xlabel = "Residuals", ylabel = "Frequency", title = "Histogram of Residuals" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### 5.3.3 Computing Predictions Next we get the predictions from the model. In this case there is an identity link function, so the prediction come directly from the linear predictor without any transformation. That is, $\hat{y} = \alpha + \beta x_i$. ::: {.callout-note} Kéry & Kellner's R code manually calculates the interval using 1.96 `(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit)`. That is an asymptotic approximation (assuming infinite degrees of freedom). Julia's predict(..., interval=:confidence) uses the exact Student's t-distribution critical value based on the model's actual residual degrees of freedom. This means Julia's frequentist ribbon will be slightly more statistically strictly correct than the manual 1.96 calculation in the ASM book (though practically, with enough data points, the visual difference is negligible). ::: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using DataFrames # Create a dense grid of x-values for prediction xpred = range(1, 16, length=100) newdata = DataFrame(x = xpred) # Get predictions and 95% Confidence Intervals directly # GLM returns a DataFrame with columns: :prediction, :lower, and :upper preds = predict(model, newdata, interval=:confidence, level=0.95) # Assemble the equivalent of pred.table pred_table = DataFrame( x = newdata.x, point_est = preds.prediction, LCL = preds.lower, UCL = preds.upper ) first(pred_table, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## 5.4 Bayesian Analysis We will translate the JAGS version of the linear regression model into a Bayesian analysis using Julia's Turing package. Now we start to see some major differences between the way you would approach this in BUGS/JAGS and how you do it in Turing (or more generally using a HMC/NUTS sampler). In the JAGS code, you put everything into the model block, including priors, likelihood, posterior predictive checks, derived residuals, etc. In Turing, this would break the NUTS sampler. In JAGS, the model string is a scripting language telling JAGS what nodes to track during its Gibbs sampling loops. In Turing, the @model macro defines a strict probabilistic log-density target for the sampler. Everything else, residuals, fit statistics, predictive datasets, etc, is just standard Julia code applied to the resulting DataFrame or Chain. Since Julia is fast, we don't have to convert this into a different language such as C++. NB the `@.` macro at the start of a statement just means to broadcast each of the operations element-wise over arrays. You can also, (and you see I do) just add the `.` broadcast operator for each one. ::: {.callout-note} The Turing philosophy is: fit the parameters in the model, generate predictions outside the model. ::: ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Turing, FlexiChains, MCMCDiagnosticTools @model function linear_regression(x, y) # Priors. tau = 0.0001 is sd = 100 α ~ Normal(0, 100) β ~ Normal(0, 100) σ ~ Uniform(0, 100) # Likelihood μ = @. α + β * x y ~ product_distribution(Normal.(μ, σ)) end model = linear_regression(x, y) chains = sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 10000, 4; progress=false) ``` ::: ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} summarystats(chains) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: These figures closely match the output from JAGS. Now we can check for convergence. ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot(chains; size=(800,600)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ### 5.4.2 GOF and Posterior Predictive Checks To replicate the `fit` and `fit.new` discrepancy measures from JAGS, we extract the posterior samples and calculate the sums-of-squares in standard Julia. This approach is lightning-fast and mathematically identical to the JAGS output. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Extract parameter vectors from the chain α_post = vec(Array(chains[:α])) β_post = vec(Array(chains[:β])) σ_post = vec(Array(chains[:σ])) S = length(α_post) # Number of posterior draws fit = zeros(S) # Sum of squares for actual data fit_new = zeros(S) # Sum of squares for new data # Generate y.new and compute discrepancies for every posterior draw for s in 1:S # Expected values for this iteration μ = @. α_post[s] + β_post[s] * x # Generate replicate dataset y_new = rand.(Normal.(μ, σ_post[s])) # Calculate squared residuals fit[s] = sum((y .- μ).^2) fit_new[s] = sum((y_new .- μ).^2) end # Calculate the Bayesian p-value (proportion of times fit_new > fit) bp_val = mean(fit_new .> fit) println("Bayesian p-value: ", round(bp_val, digits=3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bayesian p-value: 0.549 ``` ::: ::: As with the book, we have a value close to 0.5, so a decent fit. ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Replicate the JAGS goodness-of-fit scatter plot scatter(fit, fit_new, color = (:black), markershape = :circle, markerstrokewidth = 0, xlabel = "Discrepancy actual data (fit)", ylabel = "Discrepancy replicate data (fit.new)", title = "Bayesian p-value = $(round(bp_val, digits=3))", legend = false, framestyle = :box, aspect_ratio = :equal # Keeps the 1:1 line perfectly diagonal ) # Add 1:1 reference line min_val = min(minimum(fit), minimum(fit_new)) max_val = max(maximum(fit), maximum(fit_new)) plot!([min_val, max_val], [min_val, max_val], color=:red, linewidth=2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Finally, we will plot the Credible Intervals (CRI) like figure 5.4 in the book. First obtain predictions and calculate offset distances for the plot ribbon. Note that in R the plots are built using polygon and absolute values. In Julia we use the ribbon keyword and provide the lower and upper offsets relative to the mean prediction. ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Statistics # Matrix of predictions: rows = length(xpred), cols = number of MCMC draws predictions = [α_post[s] + β_post[s] * xp for xp in xpred, s in 1:length(α_post)] # Calculate Bayesian point estimates (post. means) and 95% CRI BPE = vec(mean(predictions, dims=2)) LPB = [quantile(row, 0.025) for row in eachrow(predictions)] UPB = [quantile(row, 0.975) for row in eachrow(predictions)] # Calculate offset distances required by Plots.jl 'ribbon' BPE_rib_lower = BPE .- LPB BPE_rib_upper = UPB .- BPE ``` ::: Now we can recreate figure 5.4 ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # Base plot: Raw data p = scatter(x .+ 1989, y, xlabel = "Year", ylabel = "Prop. occupied (%)", ylims = (25, 50), color = :black, fillalpha = 0.5, markershape = :circle, # pch = 16 markersize = 6, # cex = 1.5 markerstrokewidth = 0, framestyle = :axes, # frame = FALSE legend = :bottomleft # Places legend automatically ) # CIs from frequentist inference with GLM/lm() (Section 5.3.3) # Requires calculating offsets: freq_lower_dist = freq_fit .- freq_lower, etc. freq_fit = pred_table.point_est freq_lower_dist = freq_fit .- pred_table.LCL freq_upper_dist = pred_table.UCL .- freq_fit plot!(p, xpred .+ 1989, freq_fit, ribbon = (freq_lower_dist, freq_upper_dist), color = :blue, fillalpha = 0.1, # rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.1) linewidth = 2, label = "Maximum likelihood" ) # CRIs from Bayesian inference plot!(p, xpred .+ 1989, BPE, ribbon = (BPE_rib_lower, BPE_rib_upper), color = :red, fillalpha = 0.2, # rgb(1, 0, 0, 0.2) linewidth = 2, label = "Posterior inference" ) display(p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## 5.7 Maximum Likelihood Estimation We will do a more-or-less direct translation of the R code for maximum log-likelihood estimation into Julia. ::: {#28 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Optim # Define the NLL function function NLL(params, y, x) α = params[1] β = params[2] σ = exp(params[3]) # convert from log scale n = length(y) # Vectorized calculation using Julia's broadcasting dot (.) syntax μ = @. α + β * x LL = logpdf.(Normal.(μ, σ), y) return -sum(LL) end # Minimize the NLL to find MLEs inits = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Wrap NLL in a function for Optim objective(params) = NLL(params, y, x) # Run optimization using BFGS # Autodiff is optional but highly recommended in Julia for exact gradients out5_7 = optimize(objective, inits, BFGS(), autodiff = AutoForwardDiff()) # Extract parameters # Optim.minimizer returns the optimal parameters diy_params = Optim.minimizer(out5_7) diy_est = [ diy_params[1], # alpha diy_params[2], # beta diy_params[3] # log.sigma ] # To get the Standard Errors (SEs), you can extract the inverse Hessian: # hessian = ForwardDiff.hessian(objective, diy_params) # ses = sqrt.(diag(inv(hessian))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 40.74259614225698 -0.6907222556084501 1.4548947065085656 ``` ::: ::: Once again we have a close match with the R DIY-MLE output That concludes Chapter 5. I haven't tried to reproduce all the DHARMa output nor all of the plots, but we have covered most of it.
